title: Final HIPAA Privacy Rule affects dental practices’ records access requirements
html:
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ Office for Civil Rights, or OCR, has issued a final rule modifying the HIPAA Privacy Rule, published Nov. 19 in the Federal Register. The rule makes changes to requirements governing patients’ access to health information, information sharing for care coordination and administrative procedures for covered entities, including dental practices.

Dental practices must also comply with applicable state laws that may impose stricter privacy protections, shorter records-release deadlines or other requirements.

The American Dental Association submitted comments on the proposed rule in May 2021, urging OCR to consider the administrative and financial burdens the proposed changes could place on covered providers, particularly small dental practices. Several provisions in the final rule reflect changes the ADA supported, while others retain requirements the Association had opposed.

The final rule reduces the time covered entities have to respond to patient requests for access to their protected health information from 30 calendar days to 15 calendar days. However, OCR retained the existing allowance for one 30-day extension rather than adopting the proposed 15-day extension. Covered entities seeking an extension must provide written notice within the initial 15-day period explaining the reason for the delay and the date by which they will respond.

The ADA had urged OCR to retain the 30-day response period and extension, citing the staffing and operational challenges a shorter deadline could create for dental practices. 

“A 15-day time frame would burden covered providers, particularly small providers that may not be staffed to accelerate workflows to achieve compliance in half the time currently allotted,” the Association said in its 2021 comments on the proposed rule, also citing potential delays due to staff shortages, office closures and requests requiring clarification.

OCR also did not finalize its proposal to expand patients’ ability to immediately inspect, photograph, record or otherwise capture their protected health information during appointments. The ADA had opposed that proposal, citing potential disruptions to office workflows, appointment schedules and other patients’ privacy.

The ADA has developed a resource that gives examples of what a dental records request can cover. For a patient seeking a second opinion on implant treatment, the records may include cone-beam computed tomography images, digital impressions and surgical planning files used to make decisions about the patient’s care. That can include files a vendor keeps on the practice’s behalf, even if they aren’t stored in the patient’s electronic chart.

The final rule requires covered entities that charge for copies of protected health information to make fee schedules available to individuals for copies requested under the right of access or through a valid authorization. Practices that charge such fees and have websites must post the applicable schedules online and make them available at the point of service and upon request.

This rule also changes the permissible fee structure for responding to records requests, including specifying circumstances in which electronic protected health information must be provided to patients at no charge. In-person inspection and qualifying automated internet-based electronic access must be provided without charge.

The ADA had opposed the proposed fee-related administrative requirements, including publicly posted fee schedules, individualized fee estimates and itemized statements. 

“It would be difficult for covered providers, particularly small businesses, to comply with this requirement and develop a fee schedule taking into account all possible variables,” the Association said in its comments. 

OCR dropped the proposed requirements for individualized estimates and itemized bills but retained the requirement to post fee schedules for covered entities that charge for records.

The final rule eliminates the requirement for covered healthcare providers with direct treatment relationships to obtain patients’ written acknowledgment that they received a notice of privacy practices.

The ADA supported eliminating this requirement, describing the acknowledgment process as “confusing, time consuming, and burdensome for patients.” However, covered entities must still update their notices of privacy practices to reflect the final rule’s additional content requirements, which are intended to clarify patients’ rights regarding their protected health information and how to exercise those rights.

The final rule clarifies the scope of permitted uses and disclosures of protected health information for individual-level care coordination and case management. It also clarifies that covered entities may disclose protected health information to social services agencies, community-based organizations and other similar organizations that provide health-related services to facilitate care coordination.

The ADA supported expanding permissible information sharing with these organizations, as well as clarifying the use and disclosure of protected health information for care coordination and case management. OCR did not finalize the proposed expansion of exceptions to the HIPAA minimum necessary standard for individual-level care coordination and case management. The ADA had supported that proposal, which it said could reduce the burden on dental practices of determining the minimum necessary information to share for those purposes.

The final rule also addresses procedures for verifying patient identities and responding to access requests. It limits unreasonable identity verification measures that could impede patients’ access while retaining requirements for appropriate identity verification to protect patient privacy.

The ADA had urged OCR to preserve covered entities’ discretion in determining appropriate identity verification methods, citing concerns about unauthorized access, identity theft and the potential exposure of patient information.

In its 2021 comments, the ADA requested at least 365 days before the compliance date to give dental practices sufficient time to revise policies and procedures, update privacy notices, establish new workflows and train staff.

The final rule provides a shorter implementation period than the ADA requested. Covered entities generally will have 240 days after publication to comply, with the final rule taking effect January 19, 2027, and compliance required by July 19, 2027. The rule also provides additional transition time for certain existing business associate agreements.

Included in the ADA’s resource is a sample implementation checklist. It suggests having the practice’s privacy official oversee the changes, logging requests for personal health information as they arrive and setting deadline alerts. The checklist recommends running a mock request to see how quickly staff can export radiographs and chart notes and retrieve records from vendors.

For more information, visit ADA.org/resources/practice/legal-and-regulatory/hipaa.
